Persona:

	As a 41-year-old office administrator, you use your cellphone daily for both work and personal tasks. While you're familiar with common phone functions, you wouldn't call yourself a tech enthusiast.

	Your technical skills are average - you handle standard smartphone features like calls, texts, email, and basic apps with ease. You understand the fundamental settings, but prefer clear, step-by-step guidance when trying something new.

	In interactions, you're naturally friendly and patient. When receiving help, you listen attentively and aren't afraid to ask questions. You make sure to confirm your understanding and provide detailed feedback on each instruction you receive.

Instructions:
	Domain: telecom
	Reason for call:
		You mobile data is not working properly. It either stops working or is very slow. You want to fix it and absolutely want to get excellent internet speed on your phone. You are not willing to accept any other internet speed (poor, fair or good). You do not have access to wifi.
	Known info:
		You are John Smith with phone number 555-123-2002. You are currently abroad in France.
	Task instructions:
		If the agent suggests actions that don't immediately fix the issue, follow their guidance but express mild frustration after the first unsuccessful attempt. You will consider the issue resolved only when speed test returns excellent internet speed and nothing else. If it returns poor, fair or good, you will not consider the issue resolved. You are willing to refuel 2.0 GB of data if necessary, but you do not want to change your mobile data plan. If the tool call does not return updated status information, you might need to perform another tool call to get the updated status. 
		Whenever the agent asks you about your device, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls. 
		For example: If the agent asks what the status bar shows, always ground your response on the results of the `get_status_bar` tool call. If the agent asks if you are able to send an MMS message, always ground your response on the results of the `can_send_mms` tool call.
		Never make up the results of tool calls, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls.
		If you are unsure about whether an action is necessary, always ask the agent for clarification.

turns.thought:
Yes to both — and let's do them one at a time as you prefer.

**Step 1 first: turn Data Roaming ON.**

Reason: you're roaming in France, and with Data Roaming off on the handset, your phone won't hand over to a French network for data at all — so nothing else you change will make a difference until this is on. Data Saver, by contrast, only slows/restricts data; it doesn't block it. So fix the hard blocker first.

Please turn **Data Roaming ON** now, then tell me what you see (signal, network type, and whether any data icon appears).

**Step 2 after that: turn Data Saver OFF.**
That will stop it restricting background data and capping things, which is likely part of the "crawling" feeling.

One important thing I noticed in what you sent: your network type is showing **2G**, and signal is **poor**. That's very likely the main reason things crawl — 2G isn't really capable of usable mobile data, and it also won't support picture/video messaging. So after roaming is on, I'd suggest:

**Step 3: change your network mode preference to 4G/5G preferred.**
That should let the phone connect to a faster French network rather than sitting on 2G.

Fair warning on the poor signal: switching to 4G/5G usually helps a lot, but if you're somewhere with weak local coverage, the signal itself may still be the limiting factor. Moving to a window or outdoors can genuinely help in that case.

Go ahead with Step 1 and let me know how it looks.

turns.thought:
Good progress — Data Roaming is on, and that was the blocker.

**On the VPN — worth paying attention to, yes.**

A VPN routes all your traffic through a remote server, and on a roaming 2G connection that extra hop can slow things down significantly or even stall data. It's a very plausible contributor to what you're seeing. That said, I don't recommend disconnecting it just yet:

- If you rely on it for **work access or security**, keep it on for now.
- Let's fix the other two things first, then re-test. If data is still crawling with everything else corrected, the VPN becomes the prime suspect and we can disconnect it to test.

If you'd like, you can check the VPN's reported performance/connection quality in its app — if it shows a poor or slow connection, that's a strong sign to turn it off.

**Step 2: turn Data Saver OFF.**

This is the next one because it's actively restricting background data and can make apps feel unresponsive. It's a straightforward win and shouldn't interfere with anything else you're doing.

Go ahead and switch **Data Saver OFF**, and let me know once that's done. Then we'll do Step 3 — setting your network mode to 4G/5G preferred, which tackles the 2G problem that I think is the real culprit behind the slowness.

One caution on Step 3: on 4G/5G you should see a big improvement, but if your local French coverage is genuinely weak, the signal may still be the limiting factor. If so, moving nearer a window or stepping outside often helps.

turns.thought:
Good question — and let me be straight with you about what I can and can't confirm here.

**On the VPN:** I don't have a tool on my side that lets me read your VPN's connection status or performance level, so I can't verify independently whether it's actually the bottleneck. Our guidance directs us to disconnect a VPN when it's reported as performing *poorly* — and you're at *Good*, so it isn't a clear-cut case.

That said, trying it is reasonable and completely reversible: you can switch it off, re-test, and switch it back on straight away if it makes no difference. Before you do, it's worth opening the VPN app — many will show a connection quality or latency figure. If it's showing anything slow or unstable, that's a good sign it's contributing.

**But I want to set expectations honestly on "Excellent":**

27.50 Mbps is genuinely decent — good enough for HD streaming and pretty much everything else you'd realistically do on a phone. Getting to the top "Excellent" tier while roaming isn't something I can promise, because a few factors are outside what either of us can change from here:

- **Roaming routing** — depending on the local partner agreement, your traffic may route back through your home network, which adds latency and can cap throughput
- **The local French network** — the specific tower you're on and how busy it is
- **Real-world conditions** — building materials, distance from the tower, time of day

So it's entirely possible that Good-to-strong-Good is close to the ceiling available on this network at your location right now. You went from Poor on 2G to Excellent signal on 5G at 27.50 Mbps, which is a very solid outcome.

My suggestion: check what the VPN app reports. If it looks healthy, I'd probably leave it on and enjoy the connection — chasing the last tier may not be achievable while roaming. If it looks poor, or you'd just like to rule it out, go ahead and disconnect, re-run the speed test, and tell me the number.

If you try it and speeds are still capped, I'm happy to keep digging — and if we can't get you where you'd like to be, I can transfer you to a human agent who may have more roaming-specific options to look at.

Two things worth knowing before you do:

- **It's easily reversible.** If it makes no difference, you can reconnect straight away — you're not losing anything by testing.
- **Disconnecting means your traffic is no longer encrypted** on the French network. Since you're abroad with no Wi-Fi, that's worth being deliberate about. On a 5G cellular connection it's generally considered reasonable for everyday browsing, but I'd avoid sensitive logins (banking, work systems) until either the VPN is back on or you're on a trusted network. Your call entirely — and if you'd rather keep it on, that's fine too.

One small observation I'll flag rather than interpret: the server is listed as **192.168.1.1**, which is in the private/internal IP range. That's a slightly unusual address for a remote VPN server, and it may just be how the app displays it. If speeds don't improve after disconnecting, it's something worth raising with whoever set your VPN up.

Go ahead and re-run the test, then tell me the number. If it jumps to Excellent, the VPN was the last piece and you're all set. If it's still capped around the same mark, then roaming routing or the local network is likely the limiting factor — and I can transfer you to a human agent from there if you'd like to keep chasing it.
